item.title: Key plenum to advance full, rigorous Party self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27 00:04:00
Photo:Xinhua The 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) started its fifth plenary session in Beijing on Monday morning. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, delivered a work report on behalf of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and expounded on a draft decision of the CPC Central Committee on some major issues concerning strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The draft decision summarizes the achievements and experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era in a truth-seeking manner, and offers in-depth analysis of the situation and tasks concerning Party building at present and for some time to come. It also sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance with perseverance, according to a Political Bureau meeting in September that decided to submit the document to the plenum for review, Xinhua reported. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the full and rigorous Party self-governance has made significant progress, opened up a new frontier for the century-old Party in self-reform, and brought about historic achievements and transformations in the cause of the Party and the country, said an earlier Political Bureau meeting in July that set the plenum's agenda. The meeting said the Party and the people have won the historical initiative to build a strong Party and country, but noted that as profound changes unfold in the world, in China and within the Party, efforts to exercise full and rigorous Party self-governance also face many new circumstances and challenges. It called for adopting higher standards and taking more concrete measures to uphold and apply the valuable experience of full and rigorous Party self-governance in the new era, resolve the prominent issues facing Party building, and consolidate and develop the sound political environment created through Party self-supervision and self-governance. Chinese observers said the plenum underscores the CPC's determination to sustain rigorous Party self-governance as China enters a crucial stage of its modernization drive. Maintaining effective governance requires the Party to continuously address the challenges faced by the CPC, while ensuring that institutional reforms translate into stronger governance capacity, sustained economic and social development, and tangible improvements in people's lives. Maintaining vigor As China enters the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), a critical stage in laying the groundwork for basically achieving socialist modernization by 2035, the CPC faces severe challenges: strengthening its governing capacity, staying connected with the people, guarding against complacency and resolutely combating corruption, read a Xinhua commentary. Only through strong Party leadership and unwavering commitment to full and rigorous self-governance can central leadership decisions be fully implemented and the country's long-term development stay on course. History has shown that maintaining rigorous Party governance requires a long-term commitment, particularly in the fight against corruption. Any relaxation or inconsistency in anti-corruption efforts risks allowing entrenched problems to resurface, potentially undermining years of progress, Dong Yu, executive vice dean of the China Institute for Development Planning at Tsinghua University, told the Global Times. For China to achieve its long-term modernization goals, preventing corruption from taking root is therefore not merely a matter of political discipline, but a broader governance imperative, said Dong, noting that seen in this light, China's continued anti-corruption drive is about more than addressing immediate problems. It is also an effort to strengthen the institutional foundations needed to sustain the country's development over the long term. In December 2012, the CPC central leadership introduced a code of conduct, known as "eight-point rules," in a bid to strengthen Party self-governance. It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power. It has become a cornerstone of the CPC's efforts to ensure integrity, discipline and public trust. Also since 2012, the Party has pressed ahead with a rigorous anti-corruption campaign targeting high-ranking officials, misconduct at the grassroots level and corruption involving officials who have fled overseas. Some of the most senior officials - including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice, according to an article by Xinhua. In its crackdown on high-ranking officials, commonly known as "hunting tigers", more than 500 centrally managed officials were placed under investigation between the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012 and the eve of the 20th CPC National Congress in 2022. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision (NCS) launched investigations into 87 such officials in 2023, 92 in 2024 and 181 in 2025, according to an article published by Xinhua on Monday. The campaign has also targeted lower-level corruption, an effort known as "swatting flies". In 2025 alone, the CCDI and NCS directly investigated or oversaw 8,116 cases involving misconduct and corruption affecting ordinary people. Nationwide, authorities investigated 967,000 such cases, imposed disciplinary penalties on 627,000 people and referred 22,000 people to prosecutors, according to the Xinhua report. Rigorous Party self-governance is intended to strengthen the CPC's governing capacity by addressing practical challenges, refining its approach to governance and improving its ability to navigate risks, advance reforms and pursue the country's modernization goals, Zhuang Deshui, deputy director of the Research Center for Government Integrity-Building at Peking University, told the Global Times. Zhuang said the broader aim is to ensure that the Party retains the resilience, political judgment and strategic foresight needed to make consequential decisions shaping China's future and the lives of its people at critical moments in history. To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, upholding the Party's overall leadership is imperative, analysts said. Over the past years, the strong leadership of the CPC has been the key to China's great achievements in such fields as economic, scientific and social development. Latest official data released showed China's GDP grew 4.6 percent year-on- year in the first three quarters of this year, as the economy maintained steady growth under pressure and continued shifting toward new growth drivers. Meanwhile, the country has also achieved significant results in green transformation in recent years, including building the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth. Last month, the 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal, stretching from Hengzhou in South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region to the Beibu Gulf, officially opened. It is the first nationally planned and coordinated canal project since 1949 to connect an inland river with the sea, providing southwestern China with its shortest, most cost-effective and most convenient route to the sea. Global significance By steadily tackling these problems faced by the CPC, China is also creating a more transparent environment for international cooperation. The "rigorousness" in official documents must be translated into a level playing field where merit and the rule of law prevail over connections and bribery. It is hardly surprising that many foreign observers have said that the CPC's ability to reform itself is a key factor in its success, reads the Xinhua commentary. The 20th Central Committee of the CPC's fifth plenary session has also been closely watched by foreign media outlets, with some focused more on the Party discipline theme of this session. International attention to the fifth plenary session reflects more than an interest in the country's domestic politics. It also points to growing concerns over the limitations of established governance models worldwide. Against this backdrop, China's emphasis on long-term strategic planning and policy continuity has drawn attention, particularly among other countries grappling with their own governance challenges and exploring alternative approaches, said Chinese experts. Many governance challenges around the world arise not because countries lack policies, but because institutions lack effectiveness, coordination, or public confidence. The Chinese experience suggests that governance capacity depends not only on economic resources but also on institutional discipline, accountability, and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances, Essam Sharaf, former Egyptian Prime Minister, told the Global Times in a previous interview. One of the most important lessons is that self-renewal is essential for long-term success. Institutions must regularly evaluate their performance, address shortcomings, and pursue continuous improvement. Without such efforts, even capable systems may struggle to sustain effectiveness over time, said Sharaf. "From my observations, one 'secret' of the CPC is the professionalism of officials, which is not limited to senior leaders. High-quality public management is pervasive. The CPC Central Committee's Organization Department is responsible for selecting, training, monitoring, assessing, and promoting Party and government officials - and, when necessary, demoting or firing them. The process is rigorous, quantitative and continuous," Robert Lawrence Kuhn, chairman of The Kuhn Foundation, creator and host of Closer to Truth, and a recipient of the China Reform Friendship Medal, told the Xinhua News Agency in an interview. "CPC rules on work style and personal conduct have become stricter. The Eight Rules of the Party Central Committee reject extravagance and reduce ceremonial visits, meetings and 'empty talk'. A training campaign emphasizes strict standards in morality, power and self-discipline, as well as integrity in decision-making, official conduct and personal behavior. Over more than 35 years of engaging with Chinese officials at all levels, I have generally found them to be among the most competent administrators anywhere," said Kuhn. The CPC's experience offers a valuable lesson for political parties around the world, particularly those that have governed for extended periods: sustaining effective governance depends not merely on organizational strength or institutional arrangements, but also on the ability to identify shortcomings, correct mistakes and continuously renew themselves, said Dong. The effectiveness of the CPC's self-reform and strict Party governance should therefore be assessed not only through institutional changes, but also through their tangible outcomes. The key is whether these efforts have strengthened governance, advanced economic and social development, and improved people's lives, Dong noted.

item.title: China seeks input on new rules to protect trade secrets, targeting foreign entities posing risks to national interests
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 23:43:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Monday began to solicit public opinions on draft special regulations to protect Chinese trade secrets, which proposed a range of measures, including restrictions on trade, investment and entry, against foreign entities whose infringement of Chinese trade secrets harms or poses a real threat to China's national sovereignty, security and development interests. The proposed regulations could further strengthen China's legal framework for protecting trade secrets in cross-border economic activities, providing more targeted tools to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese businesses while maintaining normal international trade and investment cooperation, Chinese experts said. Stronger legal measures Foreign entities that infringe on Chinese trade secrets in international economic and trade activities and related fields may face restrictive measures if their conduct harms or poses a real threat to China's national sovereignty, security or development interests, according to the draft regulations released on Monday. These provisions are formulated in accordance with China's Foreign Trade Law, the Anti-Unfair Competition Law and other relevant laws and regulations, with the aim of safeguarding national sovereignty, security and development interests and protecting the legitimate rights and interests of rights holders, according to MOFCOM. The public consultation will remain open until November 24, according to MOFCOM. According to the draft, MOFCOM may restrict or prohibit relevant foreign entities from engaging in goods and technology imports and exports and international services trade involving China, and prohibit exports of relevant items to these entities. Other proposed measures include restricting or prohibiting new investment in China, restricting or prohibiting the entry of relevant personnel and means of transport, restricting or revoking work permits and stay or residence status, and imposing fines in accordance with the law. The draft also authorizes MOFCOM to investigate whether relevant conduct harms China's national sovereignty, security or development interests. Enterprises, organizations and individuals may submit suggestions or report trade secret infringement involving foreign entities. The draft marks a further step in strengthening China's legal framework for protecting trade secrets in cross-border economic activities, Huo Jianguo, former head of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under MOFCOM, told the Global Times on Monday. Huo said that unlike existing regulations that mainly address general trade secret infringement, the new draft links trade secret protection to China's national sovereignty, security and development interests. It proposes restrictions on trade, investment and personnel entry against foreign entities whose infringement of Chinese trade secrets harms or poses a real threat to these interests, providing more targeted legal tools to address cross-border trade secret violations, Huo noted. Also, compared with China's existing Trade Secret Protection Provisions, which took effect on June 1 and focus primarily on preventing and addressing trade secret infringement and maintaining fair competition, the proposed rules establish a more specific framework for addressing foreign entities whose infringement also affects China's national interests. The draft also provides mechanisms for modifying or cancelling restrictions. Foreign entities that take corrective action, cease infringement, eliminate the danger and compensate for losses may apply for the measures to be modified or cancelled. MOFCOM may decide whether to maintain, suspend, modify or cancel the measures following an assessment. Under special circumstances, Chinese enterprises, organizations or individuals may also apply to MOFCOM for approval to conduct transactions with restricted foreign entities. These provisions provide flexibility in implementing the proposed measures while allowing certain transactions to proceed under specified conditions, experts said. Safeguarding security, fair competition The proposed regulations come against a backdrop of growing international disputes over intellectual property, advanced technologies and the protection of commercial information, with trade secret issues increasingly becoming a source of friction in international economic relations. The proposal comes shortly after the US imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies on October 19 over alleged trade secret theft under the so-called Protecting American Intellectual Property Act, according to a MOFCOM statement issued on October 20. In response, a MOFCOM spokesperson rejected the allegations on October 20, noting that the US had stigmatized Chinese enterprises and imposed sanctions that seriously damaged their legitimate rights and interests. The spokesperson said the rapid development of Chinese artificial intelligence companies was the result of sustained basic research, innovation investment, independent innovation and open cooperation, rather than alleged trade secret theft. MOFCOM urged the US to correct its actions, warning that China would take necessary measures to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies if Washington failed to do so. While there is no official indication that the latest draft regulations were introduced in response to the dispute, the proposal should be viewed in the broader context of China's efforts to strengthen its legal framework for foreign-related economic and trade activities, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Monday. As international competition intensifies in advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence and semiconductors, protecting trade secrets and intellectual property has become increasingly important, Hu said, adding that foreign companies engaged in normal and lawful trade, investment and technological cooperation with China would not face restrictions. "Strengthening trade secret protection is consistent with China's commitment to high-level opening-up," Hu said, noting that effective protection of trade secrets and intellectual property is essential to a stable, transparent and predictable business environment. Both Chinese and foreign companies need such protection, as a stronger legal framework would help ensure fair competition and provide clearer safeguards for international trade and investment cooperation, Hu said.

item.title: Xiong'an is turning bold ideas into reality, offering world new vision for smarter cities and better governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 21:50:00
A participant tests a robot during the 2026 Global Governance Forum in Xiong'an, Hebei, on October 23, 2026. China hosted the three-day inaugural Global Governance Forum opening Friday in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province. The event aims to pool wisdom for improved global governance, one year after China put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI). Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the forum, saying that China stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits, pool strength through confidence-building and tackle challenges through cooperation. He called for efforts to promote the implementation of the GGI to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world of turbulence and transformation, and jointly move toward a community with a shared future for humanity. At the forum, held under the theme "Rebuilding Confidence and Cooperation: Reforming and Improving Global Governance in a Transforming World," Global Times reporters witnessed lively exchanges among Chinese and international participants on how to reform and improve global governance. In a year of particular historical significance, China's governance practices and the global governance agenda found a point of convergence in Xiong'an, a young city offering a glimpse of how long-term planning, technological innovation and people-centered development can be translated into reality. Ahead of the forum's opening, international guests visited the start-up zone of Xiong'an, witnessing how the "city of the future" is taking shape. Canadian author and journalist Arnold August, on his third visit to China, was still struck by what he saw in Xiong'an. Jorge Agudero, a writer and scholar from Spain, told the Global Times that China's achievement in building Xiong'an into a technologically advanced, green and innovative "city of the future" in just over nine years was difficult for many foreigners to imagine. What impressed these visitors was more than the speed and scale of construction. Xiong'an offers a tangible example of how governance ideas can move from ambitious plans to practical results, and why China's experience is attracting attention in discussions about the future of global governance. In April 2017, China decided to establish the Xiong'an New Area as part of a strategy to promote the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. Serving as a hub to accommodate non-capital functions relocated from Beijing, the city was designed to be smart, green, innovative, livable and free from "urban ills." Long-term thinking: A lesson from Xiong'an At the forum, "global governance" and "Chinese solutions" were among the recurring themes heard by Global Times reporters. The gathering brought together nearly 400 representatives from more than 90 countries and international and regional organizations, including the UN. With participants drawn from political, academic, business, financial, technological and cultural fields, the forum reflected the growing importance of broad participation and cooperation in addressing global challenges. Global Times reporters also noticed that many international participants were particularly interested in why such a high-level forum was being held in Xiong'an, rather than in established Chinese megacities such as Beijing or Shanghai. Guy Ryder, UN Under-Secretary-General for Policy, was among those impressed by the city's development. Having recently visited Shanghai and observed its urban transformation, Ryder told the Global Times that Xiong'an offered another striking example of China's approach to planning. "I am deeply impressed by its large-scale, long-term and highly ambitious urban-planning vision," Ryder said, noting that the city's significance lies in its ability to look beyond immediate needs. "It embodies forward-looking policymaking: when tackling present-day problems, it keeps future generations firmly in mind," he said. "Few cities are built around such a consistent underlying vision and logic." Sunday marked the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the lawful seat of the People's Republic of China at the UN, a milestone with profound significance for China, the UN and the wider world. Ryder also placed his observations in the wider context of China's development and its role in the international system. He noted that China's remarkable economic achievements have benefited its people while making the country an important engine of global growth. At a time of rising protectionism and economic uncertainty, China's commitment to openness and international economic cooperation remains significant, he said. He also highlighted the connection between China-proposed initiatives and the work of the UN, citing the Global Development Initiative as an example of efforts that contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals agreed upon by UN member states. An aerial view of the Xiong'an Business Service Center in Xiong'an New Area, North China's Hebei Province Photos on this page: VCG Bring Xiong'an's achievements back home The discussion about governance was not confined to meeting rooms. At the forum venue, international visitors paused to examine displays of Xiong'an's latest technological achievements. Some interacted with locally developed robots, while others gathered around models showcasing the city's emerging industries. Among the exhibits drawing attention was a model of the "Xiong'an-1," the first satellite manufactured in the new area by Hongqing Technology. The latest milestone came on August 19, when the Xiong'an-1 was successfully launched into orbit aboard a Zhuque-3 Y2 reusable rocket from the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone in Jiuquan, Northwest China's Gansu Province. For many participants, the exhibits offered a glimpse of how a city established only nine years ago is developing advanced industries alongside its urban infrastructure. Andrea Renda, director of research at the Centre for European Policy Studies and an expert on AI governance, showed particular interest in Xiong'an's focus on physical AI - applying artificial intelligence in the real world - rather than pursuing distant technological ambitions. "I am working on similar topics in Europe, and am determined to bring some of the achievements of Xiong'an, and also any of the challenges, back home after the forum," he told the Global Times. Dr Yukteshwar Kumar, a sinologist and professor at the University of Bath in the UK, who previously served as deputy mayor of Bath, also saw wider significance in the choice of Xiong'an as the forum's host city. He told the Global Times that holding a major international event in Xiong'an demonstrated that China's capacity to host high-level global gatherings is not limited to megacities. Drawing on his experience in Bath, Kumar noted that many smaller cities overseas lack the facilities needed to host large international conferences. Against that background, he considered Xiong'an's achievements particularly impressive and expressed interest in exploring the city further. International participants' interest also extended beyond urban construction to economic and industrial cooperation. Ge Yin, an associate professor at the Institute of Economics of the Hebei Academy of Social Sciences, observed that guests from Europe and Asia were increasingly interested not only in Xiong'an's rapid development, but also in its governance model and opportunities for industrial collaboration. She cited the example of former Kyrgyz prime minister Djoomart Otorbaev, who explored the possibility of deeper energy investment cooperation during a visit to China Huaneng Group, taking into account Kyrgyzstan's rapid economic growth, energy shortages and opportunities arising from the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway project. Such exchanges, Ge said, show that Xiong'an is becoming more than a showcase of China's modernization. It is also emerging as a platform through which international visitors can better understand China's governance practices and explore practical cooperation. A community holds an event to assist elderly residents, focusing on their practical needs in digital use and home-based care in Xiong'an, Hebei, on October 16, 2026. People first: Where governance becomes tangible For Ge, the decision to hold the forum in Xiong'an allowed international discussions on governance to be connected with a real-world example. "From planning before construction to the coordinated development of 'three cities' - above ground, underground and in the cloud - and the creation of 15-minute community living circles, Xiong'an demonstrates a governance approach centered on long-term planning, integrated development and people's needs. These principles resonate with the people-centered approach advocated by the GGI." During previous visits to local communities, Global Times reporters observed how the city's digital management systems are being connected with neighborhood services. From centralized urban management through its computing center to rapid community-level response mechanisms, the underlying idea is consistent: technology is a tool, while people remain the ultimate purpose of governance. Community workers make regular visits to elderly residents living alone, while digital systems help identify situations that may require additional attention. These details may not feature prominently in speeches at an international forum, but they offer a concrete picture of what people-centered governance can mean in practice. Over the past nine years, around 170,000 residents have been relocated and resettled in an orderly manner, while more than 81,000 new urban jobs have been created. The concept of a 15-minute public service circle has also been translated into neighborhood facilities and services. Joseph Olivier Mendo'o, head of the African Youth Delegation in China, told the Global Times that before arriving, he had known the city mainly through reports and photographs. He imagined a large-scale construction project filled with new infrastructure, perhaps lacking the everyday atmosphere of an established community. What he saw during a visit to the Rongdong area, a resettlement community for local residents, challenged that impression. Residents were taking walks along green corridors, while schools, community service centers and commercial facilities had been developed alongside modern residential buildings. A local resident told him how his family had moved from their original village into modern housing, gaining a better living environment while retaining connections to their local heritage and community memories. "This showed that modernization need not be measured solely by the scale of buildings or the speed of construction," he said. Such firsthand experiences, he believes, demonstrate that developing countries can explore their own paths to modernization in line with their national conditions. Xiong'an's experience, he added, "should not be seen as a miracle belonging exclusively to China, but as a source of inspiration for other developing countries." Even with limited resources, he suggested, sound planning and a commitment to people's well-being can help people build modern cities suited to their own societies. "I would encourage more young Africans to come here, to learn, exchange ideas and find inspiration for Africa's own development," he said. In this young city, where ambitious planning meets everyday life, the discussions on global governance found a fitting setting - one that invites the world to consider not only how cities and institutions are governed, but ultimately whom governance is meant to serve.

item.title: 2,054 aftershocks recorded after magnitude-7.0 earthquake in Baqen as geo-analysis on 80 glacial lakes and 145 glaciers unfolds
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 20:13:00
Power workers install electricity connections for prefabricated shelters at a temporary relocation site in Maru Township, Baqen County in Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, on October 25, 2026. Photo: IC Following the magnitude-7.0 earthquake in Baqen County of the city of Nagqu, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, 2,054 aftershocks had been recorded as of Monday morning. Rescue and relief operations are progressing steadily to ensure basic food and water supplies and support the orderly resumption of normal life and production in affected areas, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Monday. According to the China Earthquake Networks Center, among the aftershocks, 10 measured magnitude-4.0 to -4.9, and two measured magnitude-5.0 to -5.9. No aftershocks of magnitude-6.0 or above had been recorded. The strongest aftershock measured magnitude-5.7, with its epicenter 19 kilometers from that of the main quake. Rescue operations are progressing steadily. The Chinese People's Armed Police Force Xizang Corps having searched 475 households across seven villages in the Maru Township area as of 3 pm Sunday and providing medical assistance. Rescue workers continue to provide hot meals and drinking water to affected residents, meeting their basic needs and supporting the orderly restoration of normal life and production in the earthquake-hit areas. Gangqie Township, one of the areas hit hardest by the earthquake, is stepping up efforts to relocate affected residents and distribute cold-weather supplies. Seventeen temporary shelters have accommodated more than 900 households. At a temporary shelter in a village in Gangqie Township, 200 prefabricated houses are being built to ensure that affected residents can move in as soon as possible. Local authorities have also deployed emergency teams to inspect buildings, identify safety hazards and classify damaged homes, providing a basis for future repairs and reconstruction. Peng Jie, a volunteer from South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region who traveled for two nights and three days to reach the earthquake-hit area in Xizang, told the Global Times on Monday that he arrived on Sunday and spent the night in his own tent, enduring temperatures of around -10C. With the initial search-and-rescue operations largely completed, relief efforts have shifted toward providing shelter and daily necessities for affected residents. Drawing on his experience as a survivor of the magnitude-8.0 quake that hit Wenchuan of Sichuan in 2008, Peng said he hopes to provide psychological support to survivors, many of whom may be struggling with anxiety over aftershocks or the loss of family members. He plans to share practical safety advice on how to respond to aftershocks. Through one-on-one conversations and emotional support, he hopes to help affected residents overcome their fears and regain confidence, Peng said. Following the Baqen earthquake, China's Ministry of Natural Resources has completed inspections of potential geological hazard sites within 50 kilometers of the earthquake's epicenter and is continuing to monitor the risk of secondary geological disasters, CCTV reported on Monday. The ministry has activated a Level III geological disaster response and sent additional experts to the earthquake-hit area to assess potential secondary geological hazards with local teams. Remote-sensing analysis of 80 glacial lakes and 145 glaciers within 50 kilometers of the affected area found that the earthquake had limited overall impacts on them, with no earthquake-triggered glacial lake outburst disasters detected so far.

item.title: A cyclone to hit Himalayas and bring extreme snowfall to Xizang region? China's meteorological authority debunks rumors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 14:31:00
Sunrise over the snow-capped peaks of the Himalayas Photo: IC The China Meteorological Administration (CMA) on Monday debunked online claims that a tropical cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal between October 26 and October 31 would "slam into the Himalayas" and bring exceptionally heavy snowfall to the southwestern part of China's Xizang Autonomous Region, clarifying that the storm could affect southern Xizang but that the description of the online claims was inaccurate. According to Dong Lin, chief forecaster at China's National Meteorological Center (NMC), a tropical depression is currently active over the Bay of Bengal and is expected to intensify into a cyclonic storm on Monday, with its strength comparable to the tropical storm category used in China. After forming, the storm is forecast to move westward initially and continue to intensify, potentially reaching the level of a very severe cyclonic storm, with sustained winds of 33 to 38 meters per second. The storm is expected to make landfall along India's eastern coast on October 28 as a severe or very severe cyclonic storm before turning northward and gradually weakening, chinanews.com.cn reported. Given the limitations of the forecast period, forecasts of the storm's post-landfall track and intensity remain uncertain. By the time it approaches the Himalayas, the system is expected to have weakened into a weak residual vortex, making online claims that the cyclone will "slam into" the Himalayas inaccurate, and its main body is impossible to cross the mountain range, Dong said. The NMC forecasts notable rain and snow across central and eastern Xizang on Friday and Saturday as a Bay of Bengal storm moves northward and interacts with a plateau trough. Shannan Prefecture, Xigaze and Lhasa in Xizang could see moderate to heavy snow or sleet, while parts of the southern border may experience heavy to exceptionally heavy snowfall, with 10 to 30 millimeters of precipitation and 5 to 25 centimeters of new snow accumulation. According to Chen Tao, chief forecaster from the NMC, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau's high terrain acts as a natural barrier, preventing the Bay of Bengal storm from crossing it. The heavy precipitation and snow forecast for southern Xizang is not directly attributable to the cyclone itself crossing the mountains, Chen told the Global Times on Monday. Chen explained that on Friday and Saturday, the circulation of the northward-moving Bay of Bengal storm is expected to drive southerly winds, continuously transporting warm, moist air toward the plateau. When this moisture encounters the southern slopes of the Himalayas, it will be forced upward. The orographic uplift along the southern slopes of the Himalayas will trigger heavy rain and snow. An eastward-moving westerly trough is expected to interact with the Bay of Bengal storm, boosting moisture transport and atmospheric uplift and intensifying precipitation. The storm's circulation is forecast to weaken on November 1, bringing a significant reduction in rain and snow across southern Xizang, Chen said. According to Chen, the storm's evolution will be influenced by the westerly trough, the subtropical high and South Asia's terrain. If it weakens rapidly after landfall, reduced moisture transport could alter the intensity and distribution of precipitation in southern Xizang, requiring continuous monitoring and updated forecasts. According to Dong, whether heavy snowfall occurs in southwestern Xizang will depend not only on the cyclone's track but also on the strength and position of the plateau trough, the residual vortex's intensity and moisture transport efficiency. As the forecast period is relatively long, the actual snowfall intensity and accumulation remain uncertain.

item.title: Lula's reelection expected to bring continuity to China-Brazil ties, fresh momentum for Global South cooperation: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 12:56:00
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (center) delivers a speech after winning the election in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 25, 2026. Photo: VCG "Thank you, Brazilian people," Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva wrote on social media on Sunday night after securing a historic fourth presidential term in a dramatic electoral comeback. When asked to comment on Lula's reelection victory and China's expectations for bilateral ties, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday that China takes note of the announcement by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court of President Lula's runoff victory and extends congratulations on that. China stands ready to work with Brazil to advance the building of the China-Brazil community with a shared future, he noted. Lula's victory has drawn international attention not only for its implications for Latin America's shifting political landscape, but also for the future of China-Brazil relations, with prospects for deeper economic cooperation, sustained high-level diplomatic engagement and closer coordination within BRICS and other multilateral frameworks coming into focus. With 99.96 percent of the votes counted, Lula received 51.78 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.22 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party's presidential candidate and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, according to the official tally reported by Xinhua News Agency. Lula will be sworn in on January 5, 2027, for a four-year term, marking his fourth election as Brazil's president. The victory marked the first time a presidential candidate in Brazil had overturned a first-round deficit to win a runoff election. According to Xinhua, Brazil's presidential election follows a two-round majoritarian system. To win in the first round, held on October 4, a candidate must secure more than half of the valid votes. Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of incumbent Lula, winning about 47 percent of the valid votes against Lula's roughly 45 percent. As neither candidate crossed the 50-percent threshold, the two advanced to a runoff, which Lula won. The election outcome comes amid significant political shifts across Latin America and growing geopolitical competition in the region. International media have highlighted the implications of Lula's victory for Brazil's relations with major powers, particularly China and the US, as well as the country's role in promoting cooperation among Global South nations. The South China Morning Post reported on Monday that Lula's reelection would extend the tenure of an administration under which Chinese investment in Brazil had reached record levels. Pan Deng, director of the Latin America and Caribbean Region Law Center at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection has provided stability and predictability for China-Brazil relations over the next four years. Pan said the political consensus reached by the two countries' leaders during Lula's 2023 visit to China, together with sustained high-level exchanges, has strengthened mutual trust and provided strategic guidance for bilateral ties. Despite potential constraints from a conservative Congress, cooperation with China enjoys broad support across Brazil's political spectrum and is unlikely to be significantly affected by domestic political divisions, he added. China's top diplomat Wang Yi met with Special Advisor to the President of Brazil Celso Amorim on September 16 in Beijing. Amorim said Brazil stands ready to work with China to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state and inject new connotations into building a Brazil-China community with a shared future for a more just world and a more sustainable planet, Xinhua reported. China has remained Brazil's largest trading partner for years, with bilateral economic ties forming a major pillar of the broader relationship. Trade between Brazil and China reached a record $143.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026, reinforcing China's position as Brazil's largest trading partner. Brazilian exports to the Chinese market totaled $84.7 billion between January and September, an increase of 12 percent compared with the same period in 2025. Imports from China rose 9.9 percent to $58.6 billion. The figures were released by Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services and compiled by the Brazil-China Business Council, according to a report published by Valor Econômico and covered by Brasil 247. Looking ahead, Pan identified three areas with significant growth potential for China-Brazil cooperation: green and low-carbon development, including renewable energy and environmental protection; the digital economy and artificial intelligence, particularly in agriculture and AI governance; and expanded aerospace cooperation, building on the two countries' longstanding satellite partnership to advance remote-sensing applications in agriculture, disaster prevention and logistics. Xu Shicheng, vice president of the China Society of Latin American Studies, told the Global Times on Monday that Lula's reelection could also help take China-Brazil relations to a new level, as bilateral cooperation has expanded beyond traditional commodity trade into emerging sectors such as electric vehicles, renewable energy, infrastructure and advanced technologies. Beyond specific industries, Chinese analysts also pointed out that the Lula administration's emphasis on strategic autonomy and economic development aimed at improving people's livelihoods aligns closely with China's pursuit of high-quality development and open, inclusive international cooperation. At the multilateral level, Lula's reelection is also expected to provide continuity for Brazil's participation in BRICS and broader Global South cooperation, they noted. China and Brazil could continue coordinating their positions on reform of the United Nations and World Trade Organization, global debt restructuring and international climate negotiations, helping ensure that global governance arrangements better reflect the concerns and development needs of emerging economies, Pan said. The two countries could also jointly initiate inclusive cooperation projects targeting developing nations, providing additional opportunities for Global South countries to participate in international economic and technological cooperation. Pan said such initiatives could contribute to a more equitable international development environment and strengthen the collective voice of developing countries in global affairs. The election has also attracted attention for its potential implications for Latin America's political landscape. Reuters reported that Lula's victory came against the backdrop of recent electoral gains by right-wing political forces in several Latin American countries, raising questions about how Brazil's regional diplomacy might evolve during his next term. Pan argued that Lula's victory should not simply be viewed as a return of a particular ideological camp, but rather as a pragmatic response by Brazilian voters to economic and social challenges, including high inflation and poverty pressures associated with neoliberal policies. The outcome could strengthen Latin America's pursuit of independent development and inject fresh momentum into regional integration, he said. Xu noted that Lula could face considerable domestic political challenges during his fourth term, as right-wing and center-right forces secured significant representation in Brazil's Congress. Nevertheless, he said Lula's previous poverty alleviation and social welfare policies have retained support among lower-income voters, while his administration is expected to continue prioritizing BRICS cooperation and Brazil's role in the Global South. The election also sends a message that Latin American countries can pursue development paths suited to their own national conditions rather than relying on Western-led models, while expanding diversified international partnerships, Pan said. He added that the result reflects growing regional aspirations for independent decision-making and resistance to external interference.

item.title: China's state security authority warns of data security risks from discarded industrial equipment
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26 09:45:00
Photo: China's Ministry of State Security China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) warned on its WeChat account on Monday that improperly disposed-of industrial equipment and specialized instruments could pose risks to commercial secrets, critical infrastructure and national security, as sensitive data may remain recoverable even after files are deleted or storage devices are formatted. According to the article the MSS posted, some organizations mistakenly believe that deleting files or formatting hard drives is sufficient before selling or disposing of outdated equipment. However, such operations generally remove only file indexes, leaving underlying data potentially recoverable through specialized techniques. Conventional file deletion or formatting does not necessarily erase the underlying information, the article noted. Even equipment that appears to have reached the end of its service life may still contain sensitive corporate or industry data. The risks vary across sectors, potentially affecting corporate interests, the security of critical industries and national security, according to the article. In critical infrastructure sectors such as energy, telecommunications, transportation, chemicals and water management, retired industrial control systems and programmable controllers may contain operational parameters, facility layouts and security configurations. If acquired by overseas organizations, such information could be used to identify system vulnerabilities and security weaknesses, potentially facilitating cyberattacks or physical sabotage, the MSS warned. The article also highlighted risks associated with secondhand surveying and monitoring equipment, including GPS receivers and geological exploration instruments. Such devices may retain high-precision coordinates, terrain data and mineral exploration records, potentially including sensitive geographical information related to military-controlled areas, classified facilities and strategic infrastructure projects, the MSS said. Foreign intelligence agencies could also seek to acquire discarded industrial equipment and storage media from sensitive sectors through secondhand trading platforms or recycling channels, the article warned. Such equipment could be used to recover sensitive information or reverse-engineer system architectures, control logic and security vulnerabilities. Some buyers may offer unusually high prices while specifically targeting industrial enterprises and research institutions. To mitigate these risks, the article called for stricter management of discarded equipment, emphasizing that secure data destruction should take place before devices are sold or transferred. For equipment containing critical data, physical degaussing or destruction of storage media should be prioritized to prevent information recovery, according to the article. The article also recommended using qualified recycling and disposal providers rather than casually selling industrial equipment through secondhand platforms, while ensuring that the disposal process is properly documented. It further urged organizations to exercise caution when approached by buyers offering unusually high prices for discarded equipment, and to verify their identities and qualifications. Global Times

item.title: Washington's 'shutdown' is choking off its own future: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 22:38:00
China US Illustration: Chen Xia/GT As capital from many countries flows into China at an accelerating pace, US investors - constrained by their own country's rules - can only watch as their window of opportunity narrows. Washington should listen carefully to the concerns of US farmers, pharmaceutical companies and investors, and weigh the costs of imposing restrictions. The US Treasury recently released a revised proposed rule on outbound investment restrictions inviting public comments through December 7. In addition to the existing restricted sectors of semiconductor technologies and microelectronics, artificial intelligence systems and quantum information technologies, the proposal seeks to bring supercomputing and hypersonic systems under more detailed controls, while adding biotechnology to the list and designating China and other countries as "countries of concern." On October 24, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) responded to "a recent US Treasury proposal that would expand and intensify restrictions on outbound investment in China," calling it a discriminatory move and a typical practice of overstretching the concept of national security. The proposed rules "run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state," the MOFCOM spokesperson said. China will closely follow further developments and reserve the right to retaliate, the spokesperson noted. The steady tightening of US investment controls is an attempt to contain China's emerging industries by stretching the concept of national security beyond its proper bounds. From the 2023 executive order to the expansion of the scope of restrictions through congressional legislation in 2025, and now the addition of biotechnology, the underlying logic remains consistent: to slow China's technological progress by cutting off capital flows. The irony is that biotechnology, the latest sector to be brought under the restrictions, is also one of the most active areas of mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries. One-third of the world's innovative drugs in development come from China. This year, US pharmaceutical companies such as Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb have reached licensing agreements worth billions of dollars with their Chinese partners. Meanwhile, the US pharmaceutical industry has spent months lobbying against Washington's proposed stringent investment restrictions. Under the guise of national security, what amounts to protectionism is first and foremost tying the hands of US investors themselves. Data show that Washington's policy direction is running directly counter to the market choices of most US companies. According to MOFCOM, investment from major sources including the US, South Korea, France and Switzerland continued to grow from January to September, with investment from the US increasing by 7.7 percent. Despite the political noise, most US companies are still putting their money where their confidence in the Chinese market lies. On the other hand, the 7.7 percent growth rate was significantly lower than France's 31.8 percent and Switzerland's 26 percent, showing that Washington's restrictive measures are having a negative impact on corporate decision-making. Member Survey 2026 by the US-China Business Council found that 95 percent of respondents considered their China operations to be "somewhat to very important for staying competitive globally." The direction in which the market is voting of its own accord is precisely the opposite of the direction in which policymakers are trying to pull it. Facts confirm that countries shutting their doors often end up sacrificing their own opportunities. According to the US-China Business Council survey, US exports to China fell 26 percent last year, resulting in the loss of approximately 148,000 jobs. Among US companies affected by their own country's export controls, 61 percent have watched their market share shift to competitors. International Data Corporation predicts that Washington's trade restrictions could leave the US' humanoid robotics market nearly 60 percent smaller than it would otherwise be by 2030. "Once markets are lost, they are hard to regain," US business leaders have warned. By contrast, foreign investment in China's high-tech sector increased 33.8 percent year on year from January to September, while reinvestment of profits by foreign-invested enterprises rose 4.7 percent. The magnetic pull of China's vast market remains strong and continues to grow. As capital from many countries around the world flows into China at an accelerating pace, US investors constrained by their own country's rules can only watch as their window of opportunity narrows. China-US economic and trade relationship is built on mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, and it must not be undermined by the countercurrent of politicization and securitization. The strategic guidance provided by the heads of state of China and the US, along with the cooperative ties painstakingly built by businesses on both sides, should not be eroded by a proposed rule. China-US cooperation is vital to the well-being of the peoples of both countries, to the stability of global industrial and supply chains and to the growth of the world economy. Labeling legitimate business activities as "threats" and weaponizing capital flows undermine not only business confidence but also the foundations of the international economic and trade order. The proposed rule is still at the consultation stage, and its final text has yet to be determined. The rational voices of the US business community deserve to be heard. While reserving the right to take countermeasures at any time, China will continue to counter external uncertainties through high-standard opening-up. The proposition that "investing in China means investing in the future" will only become more evident. Washington should listen carefully to the concerns of US farmers, pharmaceutical companies and investors, and weigh the costs of imposing restrictions. The ropes used to trip others up often end up binding one's own hands first. The simple truth that cooperation benefits both sides while confrontation harms both is one Washington would do well to heed.

item.title: GT Voice: Shipbuilding industry is defined by both competition and cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 21:59:00
The world's first 41,800-ton bidirectional sailing self-discharging ship delivers in East China's Jiangsu Province on July 21. Photo: Guo Yuandanz/GT New data from China's shipbuilding industry has drawn widespread media attention. China continues to lead the world in three key indicators, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) reported. In the first nine months of this year, Chinese shipyards completed 58.05 million deadweight tons (DWT) of shipbuilding output, a year on year rise of 50.7 percent. New ship orders hit 175.29 million DWT, surging 163.2 percent year on year. As of the end of September, the order backlog stood at 399.13 million DWT, up 64.8 percent from a year earlier. Notably, China's new ship orders accounted for 81.8 percent of the global market, MIIT statistics showed. These figures amount to more than a demonstration of the country's manufacturing scale. Shipbuilding is a capital-intensive, long-cycle and technology-heavy industry. When ship owners place orders, they are not simply comparing quotations. They are making decisions on fleet capacity, asset values and delivery security. Choosing a shipyard is, in effect, a vote of confidence in an entire industrial system: its suppliers, engineers, project managers, skilled workers and ability to deliver as promised. China's expanding order book reflects not only the available capacity, but also the market's assessment of its supply-chain coordination and execution. What deserves more attention than the sheer volume of orders is their structural composition. New orders are not evenly distributed across all vessel types, but are heavily concentrated in the segments with the strictest green compliance requirements and the highest technological complexity. In the first three quarters, China's global market share in new orders for green-powered ships reached 74.1 percent, 5.7 percentage points higher than in the first half of the year. This clearly signals that China's leading position in shipbuilding is evolving from the traditional strengths of scale and cost-effectiveness to new competitive edges in green technology, sophisticated vessel construction and industrial synergy. As global maritime environmental regulations tighten and alternative fuel technologies advance, fleet owners are increasingly turning to next-generation vessels powered by methanol, liquefied natural gas and ammonia. Chinese shipyards' remarkable share in green ship orders shows that their capabilities in green design, supply chain coordination and high-standard construction have won widespread market recognition. This advantage is set to prove far more sustainable than a simple cost-and-scale edge. Many foreign media outlets tend to frame the rise of China's shipbuilding sector as a zero-sum game between China and South Korea. But this narrow narrative overlooks the profound changes unfolding across the global shipbuilding industrial chain. The expansion of China's shipbuilding ecosystem has opened up new market space for South Korean component and marine equipment companies. South Korean shipbuilders can leverage China's massive delivery volume and huge supporting demand to expand exports of their high-value-added supporting products. Small and medium-sized South Korean marine equipment makers are accelerating their entry into the Chinese market, with major supporting equipment shipped from South Korea to China including hull safety monitoring systems, marine energy-saving devices and marine engine components. This deep integration not only elevates the supporting quality of Chinese-built vessels, but also gives South Korean companies direct access to the world's largest shipbuilding market. This dynamic of "competition in finished vessels, cooperation in supporting sectors" is far closer to the industrial reality than simplistic zero-sum assumptions. The South Korean shipbuilding industry is facing pressure from labor shortages and challenges from investment in US shipbuilding. Against this backdrop, the value of cooperation becomes ever clearer. Shipbuilding is a long-haul race that rewards sustained technological investment, supply chain resilience and reliable deliveries. Global decarbonization in shipping continues to open up fresh demand. China needs to consolidate its early-mover advantage in green vessels, while South Korea needs a stable export market for the components and a reliable industrial partner. The rise of China's shipbuilding industry brings more diverse, greener supply options to back up the global transition of maritime transport. For competitors such as South Korea, the competition creates some pressure on finished vessels, but it also creates opportunities for component exports, production collaboration and strategic repositioning. So, competition and cooperation has once again proved to be the perpetual norm of doing business.

item.title: Jetta's 'comeback' in China proves the move was right
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25 20:04:00
Screenshot of the Jetta M6 Photo: Jetta official website Once synonymous with rugged reliability and the brand that gave millions of Chinese families their "first car," Jetta has recently returned to the spotlight. On October 22, FAW-Volkswagen's Jetta brand unveiled its battery electric vehicle, the M6, in China. Priced at under 100,000 yuan (about $15,000) even in its top trim, the model comes equipped with advanced urban navigation on autopilot driver-assistance features. It surpassed 10,000 locked orders within just 19 hours of launch. This figure may not be staggering in China's fiercely competitive new-energy vehicle sector, yet the market response merits close attention - especially for a legacy automaker racing to embrace electrification. More than just sales performance for a single new model, it points to broader potential for China-Germany automotive industrial cooperation. Earlier, FAW and the Volkswagen Group signed a strategic cooperation agreement in Wolfsburg, Germany. Under the deal, the two sides will jointly roll out 11 China-customized models starting in 2026, spanning battery electric, plug-in hybrid and range-extender electric powertrains. Jetta's electric transformation forms an integral part of this roadmap. More than 30 years ago, the Jetta served as a bridge between German engineering quality and China's mass market. Unlike the old "German technology, assembled in China" model, the new agreement elevates the Chinese side beyond manufacturing and market execution to deep involvement in product definition and research and development (R&D), with the Chinese partner taking the lead in selected areas. German manufacturing expertise and engineering standards, paired with China's mature battery, smart-cabin and autonomous-driving solutions as well as local supply chains, create distinctive synergy. This revives the iconic national car with German roots for a new era. The Jetta M6's market reception serves as a real-world test of this collaborative framework. Beneath China-Germany automotive cooperation lies four decades of integration and mutual trust. Since the establishment of SAIC Volkswagen Automotive Co Ltd in the 1980s, which marked the beginning of joint ventures in China's passenger car industry, the partnership has continued to evolve, with successive contract renewals in recent years and increased investment in local R&D. The rationale behind the cooperation has long since moved beyond its original model. Volkswagen has built in Hefei, East China's Anhui Province its first R&D center outside Germany, with the capacity to fully develop and validate products, cutting the overall vehicle development cycle by 30 percent. A growing body of practice shows that aligned technologies, talent pools, supply chains and market demands from both countries can generate a competitive edge greater than the sum of its parts. Against various external speculations, China has demonstrated its commitment to high-standard opening-up through verifiable institutional arrangements. It rejects closed, exclusive blocs. Foreign automakers receive full national treatment on permits, standards and subsidies. Foreign brands account for one-third of sales under China renews auto trade-in subsidy program. China's Ministry of Commerce has held repeated exchanges with the German Association of the Automotive Industry, welcoming and encouraging German enterprises to deepen their footprint in China and expand local R&D and investment. It also advocates managing frictions and differences through dialogue and consultation to keep the global automotive supply chain stable and unimpeded. Jetta's electric "comeback" in China is a tangible industrial manifestation of this openness. "Volkswagen Jetta, a rational choice" remains Jetta's most classic and widely recognized tagline. Today, "Jetta electrifies, born anew" adds a solid footnote to win-win collaboration between Chinese and foreign automakers in the new-energy age. It is, truly, "a rational choice." Jetta's "comeback" in China proves this was the right move.
